How RecursiveMAS Lets Agents Collaborate Without Talking, And How to Run All Four Patterns Today

Agents pass embeddings instead of text. +8.3% accuracy, 2.4× faster, 75.6% fewer tokens.

Multi-agent systems work by making agents talk to each other in text. RecursiveMAS makes them think in latent space instead.
RecursiveMAS treats the entire multi-agent system as one recursive computation. Agents pass continuous embeddings through lightweight RecursiveLink modules, and only the final agent in the final round decodes text.
The numbers land at +8.3% average accuracy across nine reasoning benchmarks, 1.2× to 2.4× wall-clock speedup, and 34.6% to 75.6% fewer tokens passed between agents.
Availability is open. The paper landed on arXiv on April 28, 2026 with all four collaboration patterns and 19 model checkpoints released on HuggingFace at the same time. Base LLMs stay frozen. The 13M-parameter RecursiveLink module trains for an estimated $4.27.
Jiaru "Rubin" Zou

Can Agent Collaboration itself be scaled through recursion? In #RecursiveMAS, we introduce a new learning framework that casts the entire multi-agent system as a unified latent-space recursion, unlocking a powerful scaling axis for AI teams' collaboration. Website:

Context

Most new multi-agent system proposals ship without benchmarks, theoretical results, or model releases. "Recursive Multi-Agent Systems" ships with all three, authored by researchers from UIUC, Stanford, NVIDIA, and MIT. Lead contributors are Xiyuan Yang (UIUC) and
@Jiaru_Zou
(UIUC and Stanford), twelve total authors including James Zou and Markus J. Buehler. It hit #1 Paper of the Day on HuggingFace with +250 upvotes. The repo sits at +220 GitHub stars and +30 forks as of May 4.

How it works

The bottleneck in standard multi-agent systems is text. Every inter-agent handoff means decoding tokens from one agent and re-encoding them into the next, which burns latency, dilutes context, and adds compounding cost as agent count and recursion rounds grow. RecursiveMAS removes the decode-reencode cycle from intermediate rounds and keeps coordination in continuous hidden space.
The RecursiveLink module
The RecursiveLink is a two-layer projection with a residual connection that handles all coordination between recursion rounds. Two variants exist.
The Inner Link sits inside an agent and projects the last-layer hidden state back into input embedding space, letting the agent generate latent thoughts auto-regressively without decoding tokens. The Outer Link sits between agents and maps state across heterogeneous models with different hidden dimensions (Llama to Qwen, Qwen to Gemma, etc.).
Together they account for 13.12M trainable parameters, 0.31% of the total system. The residual branch is what makes the design work: in the Table 4 ablation, removing it drops MATH500 accuracy from 88.0% to 84.4%.
The loop
A recursive round runs as follows. Agent A₁ receives the input and generates m latent steps via its Inner Link, accumulating a hidden state. The Outer Link then maps that state into A₂'s embedding space. A₂ conditions on both its input and the transferred state, generates its own latent steps, hands them to A₃, and so on through all N agents. After the last agent finishes, the state passes back to A₁ through another Inner-Outer pair, closing the loop.
Multiple rounds run before any text is decoded. Only the final agent in the final round produces the textual answer. The empirical sweet spot is m = 80 latent steps per agent (Table 9): performance plateaus there.
Training (Inner-Outer Loop)
Only the RecursiveLink modules train. All LLM backbones stay frozen. Stage 1, the inner loop, trains each agent's Inner Link independently with a cosine similarity objective: pull the latent thoughts toward the embedding of the ground-truth answer. Stage 2, the outer loop, unrolls the full recursive system for n rounds and backpropagates cross-entropy on the final textual prediction through the entire trace.
The Scaled-Sequential setup runs on 15.29 GB of GPU memory, uses AdamW with learning rate 5e-4, and trains for an estimated $4.27 (Table 5). Full SFT on the same setup costs $9.67 and ends at 68.6% accuracy. RecursiveMAS lands at 74.9%.
Why it doesn't collapse at depth
Theorem 4.1 explains why text-based recursive multi-agent systems lose accuracy when you add rounds, while RecursiveMAS gains accuracy.
Text-based recursion has to project to vocabulary space at every step, and the Jacobian of that projection is dominated by the softmax covariance matrix. For low-entropy (confident) tokens, that matrix has spectral norm close to zero, so gradients shrink toward zero across recursion rounds. RecursiveMAS keeps the full hidden-state Jacobian, which has an identity term that holds the gradient norm near 1 regardless of depth. The Evidence table cashes this out: Recursive-TextMAS degrades from r=1 to r=3, RecursiveMAS climbs.

Evidence

Table 3 reports r=3 results across six benchmarks against every relevant baseline.
RecursiveMAS averages +8.3% over the strongest baseline on each benchmark. The largest gains land on AIME2025 and AIME2026 (both 86.7% vs 73.3% for the closest text-based recursive method, a 13.4-point swing) and GPQA-Diamond (+3.7 over Single-Agent Full-SFT).
The trajectory is the actual story. Recursive-TextMAS, the closest text-based equivalent, peaks early or degrades with deeper recursion: 84.2 → 84.4 → 85.8 on MATH500, 76.7 → 77.3 → 74.7 on AIME2026, 61.5 → 59.1 → 58.6 on GPQA-Diamond across r=1, r=2, r=3. RecursiveMAS climbs monotonically across the same depths: 86.3 → 87.1 → 88.2 on MATH500, 80.0 → 86.0 → 86.7 on AIME2025, 63.1 → 64.6 → 66.2 on GPQA-Diamond. Efficiency follows the same curve: 1.2× speedup at r=1 grows to 2.4× at r=3, and token reduction grows from 34.6% to 75.6%. This is Theorem 4.1 showing up in measurements.

The four collaboration patterns

RecursiveMAS is structure-agnostic. The paper instantiates four patterns, each released as a HuggingFace collection.
Sequential
Planner, Critic, Solver in series. Light setup: Qwen3-1.7B (Planner), Llama3.2-1B (Critic), Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (Solver). Scaled setup: Gemma3-4B, Llama3.2-3B, Qwen3.5-4B.
Mixture
Domain specialists run in parallel and a Summarizer aggregates their latent outputs. Math: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. Code: Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. Science: BioMistral-7B. Summarizer: Qwen3.5-2B. Outputs +6.2% over the strongest individual specialist (Table 7).
Distillation
A larger Expert (Qwen3.5-9B) and a smaller Learner (Qwen3.5-4B) interact recursively. The Learner gains +8.0% accuracy and keeps its 1.5× speed advantage over the Expert (Table 6).
Deliberation
A Reflector (Qwen3.5-4B) and a Tool-Caller (Qwen3.5-4B with Python execution and Tavily search) iteratively critique each other. The Tool-Caller gains +4.8% from the recursive coordination (Table 8).

How to get started

The repo ships with one entry point and a Python loader API. Inference works out of the box on a single CUDA device.
Install
Create a fresh conda environment and install requirements.
bash
conda create -n recursivemas python=3.10 -y
conda activate recursivemas
pip install -r requirements.txt
For the Deliberation style, drop a Tavily API key into a .env file:
markdown
TAVILY_API_KEY=your_tavily_api_key_here
Load a system
The Python API pulls every role checkpoint for a given style in one call.
python
from system_loader import load_mas_system

mas = load_mas_system(
    style="sequential_light",
    device="cuda",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

planner = mas.agents["planner"].model
critic = mas.agents["critic"].model
solver = mas.agents["solver"].model
Each style has its own HuggingFace collection: Sequential-Light, Sequential-Scaled, Mixture, Distillation, Deliberation. Every collection holds the per-role agent checkpoints plus the Outerlinks weights.
Run each style
The repo ships
run.py
as the unified entry point. One command per style. The default dataset on every command is MATH500.
Sequential, Light:
python
python run.py --style sequential_light --batch_size 32 --temperature 0.6 --top_p 0.95 --dataset math500 --seed 42 --trust_remote_code 1 --device cuda
Sequential, Scaled:
bash
python run.py --style sequential_scaled --batch_size 16 --temperature 0.6 --top_p 0.95 --dataset math500 --seed 42 --trust_remote_code 1 --device cuda
Mixture:
bash
python run.py --style mixture --batch_size 16 --temperature 0.6 --top_p 0.95 --dataset math500 --seed 42 --trust_remote_code 1 --device cuda
Distillation:
bash
python run.py --style distillation --batch_size 16 --temperature 0.6 --top_p 0.95 --dataset math500 --seed 42 --trust_remote_code 1 --device cuda
Deliberation (needs the Tavily key):
bash
python run.py --style deliberation --batch_size 16 --temperature 0.6 --top_p 0.95 --dataset math500 --seed 42 --trust_remote_code 1 --device cuda
Swap the --dataset flag to switch tasks. The repo includes hooks for AIME2025, AIME2026, GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, LiveCodeBench-v6, MBPP+, HotpotQA, and Bamboogle. What is released today is inference plus all 19 checkpoints. The full training data and pipeline are marked pending in the README.

Limitations

Interpretability and debugging. Latent coordination produces no readable per-step trace between agents. Operators cannot inspect why a given intermediate state was reached, which makes failures hard to diagnose and risky in deployments where every inter-agent message has to be auditable.
Training pipeline not open and no license shipped. Inference demos and 19 checkpoints are released. Full training data and implementation are pending per the README, and no LICENSE file is in the repo as of May 4, which blocks production reuse until the authors clarify terms.
Confidence assumption. Theorem 4.1 assumes low-entropy tokens. High-uncertainty regimes (open-ended generation, ambiguous reasoning) may not see the same gradient stability or accuracy gain.
Frozen backbones, fixed topologies. Only RecursiveLink trains. End-to-end agent fine-tuning and dynamic agent graphs are listed as future work.
Older base models. The frozen backbones tested (Qwen3, Llama 3.2, Gemma 3, BioMistral) are one to two generations behind the current frontier. Whether the same gains carry onto Qwen 3.6 or Gemma 4 is the obvious next experiment, and Theorem 4.1 is base-model-agnostic so the recipe should hold.
So the best recommendation is to adopt for fixed-pattern reasoning pipelines on math, code, science, or medical QA where token cost matters, and wait if retraining on private data or hard interpretability is the gating need.

Who benefits and who doesn't

Benefits: ML engineers running fixed-pattern reasoning pipelines on math, code, science, or medical QA who want lower latency and token cost at equal or better accuracy, researchers extending recursive language models to multi-agent settings, and teams comfortable working with open-weight base models like Qwen, Llama, Gemma, or Mistral.
Skip: teams shipping user-facing agents that require auditable per-step traces, teams running dynamic agent graphs that change topology at runtime, teams that cannot pin compatible open-weight base models, and anyone whose immediate blocker is retraining on private data.

Practitioner implication

You can now run a 4-agent reasoning pipeline at 75.6% lower token usage with frozen open-weight LLMs, now that recursive coordination is stable across depth.

Questions?

Q: Does RecursiveMAS work with closed-source models like GPT or Claude? A: No. Latent coordination needs direct access to hidden states, so it only runs on open-weight LLMs.
Q: How is this different from LoopLM or Coconut? A: Those apply recursion inside a single model. RecursiveMAS extends recursion across a system of agents through Outer Links that map state between heterogeneous models.
Q: Can practitioners retrain RecursiveLink on a new task today? A: Not yet. Inference demos and 19 checkpoints are released, but the training pipeline is still pending per the README.
